newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians say corruption here to stay.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians say corruption here to stay.

text.p: Sameh Dandiss is only in his late teens but he is sure of one thing -- corruption is rife under Palestinian self-rule and sacking the autonomy government won't make it go away.
"The main problem is that these people stole the money until they got full, and if they move them, a new person will come and steal and steal and steal until he also gets full," he said.
"If we change them, others will come," said Dandiss, eyeing the bodyguards and shiny Mercedes four-wheel-drives on the street where Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was staying on Tuesday.

Arafat is facing the biggest internal challenge to his administration in three years of limited self-rule from lawmakers out to expose a seam of corruption and mismanagement running through the Palestinian Authority.

A panel of nine lawmakers, in a report to the Palestinian Legislative Council, urged Arafat on Tuesday to dissolve his entire cabinet and recommended that at least two ministers should stand trial. Both deny wrongdoing.

The report was broadly welcomed on the dusty streets of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, where Palestinians grappling with economic hardships have grown increasingly resentful at the high life of some of their officials.
"We're paying for the (Israeli) occupation and the ministers at the same time. It's like we're paying for both. They are both an occupation," said Abdul-Rahman al-Jibrini, a Hebron merchant.
"Every one of them is making a presidency, a government and a mafia for himself," he said. "We didn't fight...the Intifada (Palestinian uprising) or get hurt for these bad people."

Arafat returned in triumph to Gaza in 1994 to set up his new Authority after decades of struggle against Israel from exile, bringing back with him many of the Palestinians who now run and staff the entity's fledgling institutions.

Tuesday's report levelled no allegations of wrongdoing against Arafat himself though there was criticism at grass-roots level at the perceived slowness of Palestinian leaders to get to grips with corruption.

"It's time Yasser Arafat deals bravely with red-handed people," said Fathy Muhammad, a 52-year-old high school teacher from Jenin, at the northern end of the West Bank. "The committee should have been formed a long time ago," he said.
An official auditor's report earlier this year found that members of the Palestinian Authority had squandered $326 million in public funds last year.
An Arafat-appointed investigative committee reported last week that no money was squandered, but that serious financial, legal and administrative violations had taken place.
Ghazi Hamad, editor of the Islamist al-Risala newspaper which is affiliated to the Hamas opposition movement, said he feared the latest recommendations would not be respected.

"I not only demand that the cabinet be dissolved but also that ministers involved in corruption cases be sued," Hamad said. "But I have doubts that such trials could take place because of the absence of the rule of law," he said.
Others said just getting the corruption out in the open inspired hope.

"I agree to wash our dirty clothes in public in order to know -- and for everybody else to know -- that we are not covering up our mistakes," said Nadia Sulaiman, a 31-year-old non-governmental aid organisation director.
